title: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
summary: How SPLADE turns BERT's MLM logits into sparse, expanded term weights, scores them on an inverted index, and uses the FLOPS regularizer to trade quality for speed.
outcomes: Explain why vocabulary mismatch hurts BM25 and how learned expansion keeps an inverted index
Compute SPLADE term weights w_j = max_i log(1 + ReLU(w_ij)) from a small logit matrix
Compute a sparse dot-product score by traversing posting lists, in bi-encoder and doc-only modes
Explain why the FLOPS regularizer balances posting lists better than L1
Choose SPLADE settings (lambda, doc-only mode, pruning, chunking) for a production engine

lessons.title: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones

blocks.md: BM25 scores a document only on the query words it literally contains, weighted by rarity and saturated by term frequency, and it runs fast because an **inverted index** maps each term to the short list of documents that contain it. Its weakness is **vocabulary mismatch**: a relevant document that says *car* gets nothing for a query that says *auto*.

Dense retrieval fixes mismatch by embedding text into a few hundred dimensions, but every dimension is non-zero, so you need approximate nearest neighbor search instead of an inverted index, and you lose exact term matching. **Learned sparse retrieval** keeps the BM25 machinery and changes only where the weights come from: a transformer writes a weight for every term of the vocabulary, almost all of them zero. The non-zeros can include terms the text never used. That is **expansion**.

We use one running example in the whole course. The vocabulary has 10 terms (real SPLADE uses the 30,522 WordPiece tokens of BERT). The document **D1** is *fix my car engine*; the query is *auto repair*. A human would call D1 relevant, yet they share no word.

blocks.title: Bag of words versus a learned sparse vector

scenes.caption: As a bag of words, D1 has 1s on fix, my, car, engine and the query has 1s on auto and repair. No column is non-zero in both, so the dot product, and the BM25 score, is exactly 0.
SPLADE replaces the 1s with learned weights for D1. Weights appear on auto, motor, repair and price, words D1 never contains: these are expansion terms (orange).
The query is encoded the same way. It keeps auto and repair and adds car, engine, motor and fix. The query now has 6 non-zeros instead of 2.
Six columns are now non-zero on both sides (green). The score is the dot product over those columns: 6.60 instead of 0. my and price stay in D1 but cost nothing here because the query weight is 0.

blocks.md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

SPLADE (SParse Lexical AnD Expansion model, Formal, Piwowarski and Clinchant, SIGIR 2021) is the best known model of this kind. It was not the first: DeepCT learned weights only for terms already in the text, doc2query appended predicted queries to documents, and SparTerm predicted weights over the whole vocabulary but needed a separately trained gate. SPLADE made the sparse representation trainable end to end with a log saturation and an explicit sparsity regularizer, the two ideas this course builds up.

blocks.question: Query: auto repair. Document: fix my car engine. Why does BM25 give this document a score of exactly 0, no matter how k1 and b are tuned?
options: Because the document is too short for length normalization
Because the IDF of auto is negative
Because BM25 needs at least two matching terms
Because BM25 only sums over query terms present in the document, and none are
blocks.explain: BM25 is a sum over query terms that occur in the document. With zero overlapping terms the sum is empty, so tuning cannot help. Expansion is what creates overlap.

blocks.question: What does learned sparse retrieval keep from BM25, and what does it replace?
options: Keeps the inverted index and dot-product style scoring, replaces hand-made term weights with learned ones that may include new terms
Keeps the dense embedding, replaces the ANN index
Keeps the BM25 formula, replaces the tokenizer
Keeps nothing; it is a re-ranker
blocks.explain: The index structure and term-at-a-time scoring stay. The weights now come from a transformer and can sit on vocabulary terms the text never used.

lessons.title: From MLM logits to one weight per vocabulary term

blocks.md: BERT is a transformer encoder (as in the transformer course) pre-trained as a masked language model (MLM): it turns each input token into a contextual vector $h_i$, and its MLM head scores every vocabulary entry as a possible word at that position. SPLADE reuses exactly that head. For input token $i$ and vocabulary term $j$ it computes a logit $w_{ij}$:

blocks.caption: transform is a linear layer with GeLU and LayerNorm, $E_j$ is the input embedding of term $j$, $b_j$ a bias. This is the MLM prediction, so it starts from a pre-trained MLM checkpoint.

blocks.md: That gives a matrix with one row per input token and one column per vocabulary term (here 4 x 10; for real BERT, N x 30,522). SPLADE v2 turns the matrix into one vector with two steps: **ReLU then log** on every cell, then **max pooling** down each column.

blocks.caption: The natural log. The original SPLADE (2021) summed over $i$; SPLADE v2 switched to max.

blocks.title: Logits for fix my car engine (illustrative values)

scenes.caption: Raw MLM logits (made-up but plausible numbers for this toy). The car row is high on car and auto; the fix row is high on fix and repair; the engine row is high on engine and motor. Most cells are negative.
ReLU sets every negative logit to 0. Already 24 of the 40 cells are exactly zero, including the whole banana and bread columns.
log(1 + x) compresses what is left: 3.5 becomes 1.50 and 3.2 becomes 1.44, while small values barely change (0.3 becomes 0.26). Large logits can no longer dominate.

Max pooling keeps the largest cell in each column (highlighted). auto comes from the car row, repair from the fix row, motor from the engine row: each expansion term is traced to the token that produced it.
Max pooling gives D1 eight non-zero weights out of ten. engine (1.50), car (1.44) and fix (1.39) are the strongest; my gets a small 0.47.
Sum pooling (original SPLADE) adds every row instead: car becomes 2.31 because fix, car and engine all vote for it. Terms that many tokens mildly support get inflated.

blocks.title: Why the log: saturation of a single logit

scenes.caption: Without the log, a logit of 8 would weigh 8 times a logit of 1. With it, the ratio is 2.20 / 0.69 = 3.2. The paper links this to log(tf) saturation in classic IR.
Negative logits stay at exactly 0 on both curves. That exact zero, not a small number, is what keeps the term out of the inverted index.

blocks.prompt: The SparTerm baseline used ReLU without the log and needed a separate gating step for sparsity. With nothing else changed, what do you expect adding log(1 + .) did to the number of non-zero weights?
blocks.reveal: It made the vectors much **sparser**. The SPLADE paper reports this was surprising: the log saturation alone already gave sparse solutions without any regularization, and with expansion plus a sparsity loss SPLADE cut the estimated FLOPS from 4.62 (SparTerm-style expansion, no log) to 0.88 at similar quality.

blocks.md: Why did max pooling help? The SPLADE v2 paper reports almost 2 points of MRR@10 on MS MARCO (0.322 to 0.340) from that single change. MRR@10 averages, over queries, 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant passage in the top 10 (0 if none). With max, each vocabulary term is scored by its single strongest supporter, much like a ColBERT-style late interaction picks the best match per query token, rather than accumulating weak evidence from every token.

Misconception: the expansion terms are synonyms. They are whatever the MLM head plus ranking training found useful. The paper's own example document about bow legs gains *leg* and *treatment*, but also *arrow* (bow and arrow) and *teeth*, with small weights.

blocks.code:
out = mlm(**tokens).logits                      # (batch, seq_len, 30522)
acts = torch.log(1 + torch.relu(out))
acts = acts * tokens["attention_mask"].unsqueeze(-1)  # padding gives 0
rep, _ = torch.max(acts, dim=1)                   # (batch, 30522), mostly zeros
blocks.caption: Same computation as the encode method of the Splade class in naver/splade (agg=max). Masking with 0 is safe under max because all activations are non-negative.

blocks.question: A token's logit for vocabulary term j is -0.7 at every position of the input. What is $w_j$?
options: Exactly 0, so term j is absent from the index entry of this text
A small positive number from the bias b_j
blocks.explain: ReLU maps -0.7 to 0, log(1 + 0) = 0, and the max over positions of zeros is 0. Exact zeros are what make the vector sparse.

blocks.question: Using the matrix above, which input token produced D1's weight for repair, and what is that weight?
options: engine, 0.64
car, 0
repair itself, 1.16
blocks.explain: The fix row has logit 2.2 on repair; log(1 + 2.2) = 1.16 beats engine's log(1 + 0.9) = 0.64. repair is not an input token at all; it is an expansion term.

lessons.title: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index

blocks.md: The relevance score is a plain dot product between the query vector and the document vector. Because both are mostly zeros, only terms non-zero on *both* sides contribute:

Add three more documents to the toy collection. Their vectors are given (assume the same encoder produced them):

- **D2** *used car price*: car 1.90, auto 0.80, price 2.10
- **D3** *banana bread*: banana 2.40, bread 2.20
- **D4** *engine repair cost*: engine 1.60, repair 2.00, motor 0.70, fix 0.90, price 0.60

The query *auto repair* encodes to car 0.83, auto 1.39, engine 0.47, motor 0.34, fix 0.96, repair 1.28.

blocks.prompt: BM25 on the raw text would match only D4, the one document containing repair. Before stepping through the index, which document do you expect SPLADE to rank first, and will D3 be scored at all?
blocks.reveal: D1 wins with 6.60, because six of its terms overlap the expanded query, and every one of those six matches exists only through expansion (on the query side, the document side or both), since the raw texts share no word. D4 is second at 4.41 and D2 third at 2.69. D3 is never scored: none of its postings lie on a query term's list.

blocks.title: Term-at-a-time scoring of auto repair

scenes.caption: Offline, every document vector is inverted: each term with a non-zero weight gets a posting (doc, weight). Our 4 documents produce 18 postings over 10 terms.
Query term car (weight 0.83) walks its posting list. D1 gets 0.83 x 1.44 = 1.20 and D2 gets 0.83 x 1.90 = 1.58.
Query term auto (weight 1.39) walks its posting list. auto is a literal query word, but an expansion term in both D1 and D2. D1 now 2.72, D2 2.69.
Query term engine (weight 0.47) walks its posting list. D4 enters the accumulator for the first time.
Query term motor (weight 0.34) walks its posting list. motor never appears in any text, only in expansions, yet it still adds 0.35 to D1.
Query term fix (weight 0.96) walks its posting list. D1 reaches 5.11.
Query term repair (weight 1.28) walks its posting list. repair is the only query word that literally occurs in a document text (D4). D4 gets 1.28 x 2.00 = 2.56.
Done: D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69. D3 (banana bread) was never touched. Only 12 postings were read, not 4 x 10 products.

blocks.md: Cost is driven by the total length of the posting lists the query touches, not by vocabulary size. Every extra query expansion term and every long posting list is extra work. That is why sparsity, especially on the query side, is the thing training must control.

Real engines store integer impacts, not floats. The naver/splade repo exports to Anserini with a quantization factor (for example 100, so 1.44 is stored as 144), and DeepImpact quantized its impacts to 8 bits with no loss it could measure. Dynamic pruning algorithms such as MaxScore and WAND then skip documents that cannot reach the top k, exactly as with BM25.

There is a cheaper variant. **SPLADE-doc** (SPLADE v2 paper) has no query encoder: the query is just its tokens, each with weight 1, and $s(q,d) = \sum_{j \in q} w^d_j$. All neural work happens at indexing time. OpenSearch calls this *doc-only mode* (its default) and the full model *bi-encoder mode*.

blocks.title: Toy scores: full SPLADE versus doc-only

scenes.caption: Full SPLADE (query expanded to 6 terms, 12 postings read): D1 6.60, D4 4.41, D2 2.69, D3 0.

Doc-only with the same document vectors: the query is just auto and repair with weight 1, so only 4 postings are read. D1 2.26, D4 2.00, D2 0.80. The order survives here because D1's own expansion already added auto and repair.

blocks.question: A query expands to 40 non-zero terms, many of them common words with long posting lists. What happens to latency compared to a 6-term expansion?
options: Nothing; the dot product is computed on the GPU in constant time
It grows roughly with the total length of the touched posting lists, so it can get much slower
It shrinks, because more terms let WAND prune earlier
It depends only on the number of documents in the collection
blocks.explain: Term-at-a-time or document-at-a-time traversal reads every posting on every query term's list (minus what pruning skips). More and longer lists mean more work, which is why query sparsity is penalized harder.

blocks.question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
blocks.explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

lessons.title: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPS regularizer

blocks.md: SPLADE is trained on MS MARCO with a contrastive ranking loss: for query $q_i$, push the score of its relevant passage $d_i^+$ above a hard negative $d_i^-$ (for example from BM25) and above the other queries' positives in the same batch (**in-batch negatives**).

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{rank} = -\log \frac{e^{s(q_i, d_i^+)}}{e^{s(q_i, d_i^+)} + e^{s(q_i, d_i^-)} + \sum_j e^{s(q_i, d_{i,j}^-)}}

blocks.md: The ranking loss alone has no reason to keep vectors sparse: more expansion usually helps recall. So SPLADE adds a sparsity penalty, separately for queries and documents, with two strengths $\lambda_q$ and $\lambda_d$ (more pressure on queries, since query sparsity drives latency):

blocks.caption: $\bar a_j$ is the average weight of term j over a batch of N texts, a smooth stand-in for the probability that term j is active.

blocks.md: Where does this come from? Paria et al. (ICLR 2020) observed that the expected cost of scoring a query against a document with an inverted index is $\sum_j p_j^{(q)} p_j^{(d)}$, where $p_j$ is the probability that term $j$ is non-zero: a term costs work only when it is active on both sides. Counting non-zeros is not differentiable, so they replace $p_j$ by the mean absolute weight $\bar a_j$. SPLADE reports this same quantity, measured on real vectors, as **FLOPS** in its tables: 0.13 for BM25 and 0.73 for SPLADE on MS MARCO.
The key is the gradient. For one weight of document $d_i$:

blocks.caption: $\ell_1$ as implemented in naver/splade: sum over the vocabulary, mean over the batch. FLOPS pushes harder on terms that carry a lot of weight across the batch.

blocks.title: Push per weight in our 4-document batch (lambda = 1)

scenes.caption: Treat D1 to D4 as one batch. The mean weight of price is 0.74 because it is active in three documents; my is active only in D1 with 0.47, so its mean is 0.117.
FLOPS pushes on price 6 times harder than on my (0.37 versus 0.059). Terms with long, heavy posting lists are the expensive ones, and they get the strongest push.
L1 pushes every active weight equally (0.25), so it cannot tell a cheap rare term from an expensive common one.

blocks.md: To watch the regularizer act, we run projected gradient descent on the batch. Simplified: a real model gets its pull toward useful weights from the ranking loss through the encoder; here a quadratic pull toward the unregularized weights stands in for it, and weights are clipped at 0 like the ReLU does.

blocks.title: D1's weights as lambda grows (simplified training)

scenes.caption: lambda = 0: the unregularized weights from lesson 2. 8 non-zeros in D1, 18 postings in the batch.
lambda = 1: price in D1 (0.26) hits exactly 0: price is the term with the longest posting list (3 documents). my (0.47) survives at 0.42 because almost nothing else uses it.
lambda = 2: Everything shrinks, frequent terms faster. car, used by D1 and D2, drops from 1.44 to 0.88.
lambda = 4: price is now gone from D4 too, so its posting list has gone from 3 entries to 1. Batch total: 16 postings.
lambda = 8: Weights keep shrinking toward 0; repair falls to 0.11 because D4 also uses it heavily. Too much lambda erases useful signal.

blocks.md: Compare at equal size. FLOPS with lambda = 4 and L1 with lambda = 2 both leave 16 postings. FLOPS removed the two weakest *price* postings (D1 and D4), shrinking the longest list from 3 to 1; L1 removed *my* and *price* from D1. The expected cost $\sum_j p_j^2$ over this batch is 1.75 for FLOPS versus 1.875 for L1: same number of non-zeros, cheaper index. The SPLADE paper reports the same pattern at scale: at equal FLOPS, the L1 models were always less effective.

scenes.caption: SPLADE follows Paria et al.: lambda grows quadratically until step T (50k in the papers), then stays constant. Early on the encoder learns to rank before it is forced to be sparse.
A short ramp applies full pressure almost immediately, when the weights are still close to the MLM's dense-ish output.

blocks.md: SPLADE is better thought of as a family than one model. The same architecture trained with different lambda values gives anything from very sparse to heavily expanded vectors. The SPLADE paper reports typical lambda values between 1e-1 and 1e-4, and a very sparse model with about 18 non-zeros per document and 6 per query still reaching MRR@10 0.296 on MS MARCO.

blocks.question: Two terms have the same weight 0.3 in a document. Term A appears in 1 document of the batch, term B in all of them with similar weights. Under FLOPS, which weight is pushed toward zero faster?
options: A, because rare terms are noise
Both equally, since the weights are equal
B, because its mean weight across the batch is larger, so its gradient 2 a_j / N is larger
Neither; FLOPS only acts on queries
blocks.explain: The FLOPS gradient for a weight is proportional to the term's batch mean. B is active everywhere, so its posting list is long and its push is strong. L1 would treat A and B the same.

blocks.question: After raising lambda_q a lot, MS MARCO MRR@10 drops slightly but queries are much faster. What most likely changed?
options: Document vectors got denser
The vocabulary shrank
The ranking loss switched to L1
Query vectors have fewer non-zeros, so fewer posting lists are traversed
blocks.explain: lambda_q only penalizes the query representation. Fewer query terms means fewer posting lists to read, at some cost in matching power.

lessons.title: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production

blocks.md: The architecture has barely changed since 2021; most later gains came from training. SPLADE v2 (2021) introduced max pooling, the doc-only variant and **distillation**: a cross-encoder teacher scores (query, positive, negative) triples and the student is trained with MarginMSE to reproduce the teacher's score *margin*. Its negatives are mined with a first SPLADE model, which gives harder negatives than BM25. SPLADE++ (SIGIR 2022) added ensembles of mined negatives and initialization from a retrieval-pretrained CoCondenser checkpoint.

blocks.title: MS MARCO dev MRR@10 (first-stage retrieval, from the papers)

scenes.caption: Reported MRR@10 x 100. Lexical baselines first: BM25 18.4 and doc2query-T5 27.7 (expansion by generated queries).
Max pooling alone: 32.2 to 34.0. Distillation with mined negatives: 36.8. SPLADE++ with CoCondenser init and ensemble negatives: 38.0, in the range of strong dense retrievers.

blocks.md: The most cited strength is zero-shot transfer. The SPLADE v2 paper evaluates the readily available BEIR datasets with NDCG@10 (a ranking metric that rewards relevant documents near the top of the first 10 results). Averaged over its 14 datasets (13 zero-shot ones plus MS MARCO), DistilSPLADE-max scored 0.500 against BM25 0.440, ColBERT 0.455 and the dense TAS-B 0.435. On the 13 zero-shot datasets alone it scored 0.506, and SPLADE++ later reported 50.5 and 50.7 (x 100) on that 13-dataset subset.

scenes.caption: Average over the 14 datasets of SPLADE v2's BEIR table (13 zero-shot plus MS MARCO): the distilled SPLADE leads.
TREC-COVID (biomedical): SPLADE 0.710 is best, the dense model drops to 0.481.
Touche-2020 (argument retrieval): plain BM25 at 0.614 beats every neural model; SPLADE gets 0.364. Always evaluate on your own data.

blocks.md: **Related learned sparse models.** DeepImpact (Mallia et al., SIGIR 2021) first expands documents with doc2query-T5, then learns one impact score per document term; the query is an unweighted bag of words and the score is the sum of impacts of matching terms. uniCOIL (Lin and Ma, 2021) shrinks COIL's per-token vectors to a single ReLU weight, again with doc2query-T5 expansion, and runs on a standard Lucene index (1.3 GB for MS MARCO in their notes). SPLADE differs by learning expansion and weighting jointly in one model, on both query and document side.

blocks.title: A learned sparse pipeline in a search engine

scenes.caption: Indexing: every chunk goes through the transformer once and is stored as token-weight pairs. Elastic stores ELSER output in a sparse_vector field; OpenSearch uses rank_features.
Bi-encoder mode: the query also runs through the encoder, gets expanded, and is scored against the posting lists. Best relevance, but a transformer call per query and more terms to traverse.
Doc-only mode: the query encoder becomes a tokenizer plus fixed per-token weights. OpenSearch's default; faster, slightly less relevant.

Query pruning: drop low-weight query tokens, or score with high-weight tokens first and rescore the top documents with the rest (OpenSearch two-phase processor). The result can then be reranked or fused with a dense retriever.

blocks.md: **What the production docs say.** Elastic's ELSER is a learned sparse model trained by Elastic for English; its docs say it encodes only the first 512 tokens of a field (chunk longer text), that ELSER v2 used an improved FLOPS regularizer, and that by default Elasticsearch prunes query tokens that are both very frequent (more than 5 times the average token frequency) and low weight (below 0.4). OpenSearch added neural sparse search in 2.11, stores token-weight pairs in a rank features index, and recommends doc-only mode as the default trade-off.

Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

**Trade-offs to remember.**

- Index and latency grow with expansion; lambda, pruning and doc-only mode are the knobs.
- Indexing needs a transformer pass per chunk; BM25 needs none.
- The vocabulary is the model's WordPiece vocabulary, mostly English for BERT-based models. Rare identifiers split into subwords, so exact-code matching can still favor BM25, which is why hybrids with BM25 often add gains (SPLADE++ reports this on BEIR).
- Models are trained on MS MARCO passages; long documents must be chunked.

blocks.question: Your corpus is 3,000-token technical manuals. You index each manual whole with ELSER and recall is poor for facts near the end. Most likely cause?
options: ELSER encodes only the first 512 tokens of a field, so later text never reaches the index
The FLOPS regularizer removed rare terms
Doc-only mode ignores the document
BM25 fusion is required for ELSER to work
blocks.explain: Elastic's docs state ELSER uses the first 512 tokens of a field and recommend chunking larger fields into multiple values below that limit.

blocks.question: You need the lowest query latency on CPU-only search nodes but still want expansion. Which setup fits best?
options: Bi-encoder SPLADE with lambda_q = 0
Dense retrieval with HNSW
Doc-only sparse mode: expand documents at index time, tokenize queries with fixed weights
BM25 with doc length normalization disabled
blocks.explain: Doc-only mode keeps expansion on the document side, computed offline, and runs no transformer at query time. lambda_q = 0 would make queries denser and slower.

blocks.question: On a new dataset, SPLADE loses to BM25. Which explanation is consistent with the BEIR numbers above?
options: SPLADE cannot represent exact matches
BM25 always wins on BEIR
The FLOPS regularizer forbids matching rare terms
Learned models can underperform BM25 on some out-of-domain tasks (Touche-2020 is one), so you must evaluate per dataset
blocks.explain: SPLADE keeps exact term matching and wins on average, but on Touche-2020 BM25 scored 0.614 versus 0.364. Averages hide such failures.
